title: Helix Nebula (NIRCam image)
caption: Part of the Helix Nebula, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, A. Pagan (STScI)

recognition.text: Ranked #28 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: In this close-up, thousands of orange and gold pillars shaped like comets rise from the bottom edge, as if thin liquid had been blown up across a pane of glass. They are densest and darkest red at the bottom, where they form part of an arcing shell, and grow thinner and more golden higher up. This is a small section of the Helix Nebula, the expanding shell of gas and dust around a dying star.
Webb's image highlights these comet-like knots, along with fierce stellar winds and layers of gas that the dying star has shed. All of that material is interacting with the space around it.
The picture also captures an abrupt shift from the hottest gas to the coolest as the shell spreads outward from the central white dwarf, the small, hot core the star left behind.

understand.summary: This near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam shows the two shortest filters in blue, the next two, including molecular hydrogen, in green, and the two longest, including molecular hydrogen, in red.
understand.eye: All of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, so the colours are a mapping of wavelengths we cannot see.

explore: Bright blue stars dot the scene, a few of them showing diffraction spikes, with a few larger ones on the right side. The black of space shows through between the thinner pillars at the top.
alt: Thousands of orange and gold comet-like pillars streaming upward from an arcing shell at the bottom, with bright blue stars scattered across a black background.
